title: Diogenes throws away his cup
hook: seeing a child drink from cupped hands, he tosses away his last possession

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes and the king. Your line was stand out of my light. Did you get your minute in the sun? Day thirty-five, the end of week five.
screen: `DIOGENES AND THE KING — STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Somewhere in a kitchen near you there's a junk drawer. Old chargers for phones nobody owns anymore. Keys to nothing. A takeout menu from a place that closed. Now a man whose whole junk drawer, whose whole house, whose everything, fits in a small bag over his shoulder. A cloak, a stick, a bag, and a cup for drinking. That was Diogenes, the Cynic who told Alexander to move out of his sunlight. And one day he watched a child get a drink of water, and lost one more thing.
screen: `A DRAWER FULL OF KEYS TO NOTHING.` → `A CLOAK, A STICK, A BAG, A CUP.` → `A CHILD, DRINKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Diogenes Laërtius tells it. Diogenes sees a child drinking water from his cupped hands. And Diogenes pulls the cup out of his bag and throws it away, saying something like: a child has beaten me at living simply. The same source tells a twin story: seeing a boy who'd broken his bowl eating lentils out of a hollowed piece of bread, Diogenes threw away his bowl too. Notice who the teacher is. Not a philosopher. A child. Someone who didn't know that you're supposed to need a cup. Diogenes, the man who owned almost nothing, still found something to put down. Now, careful. This is a story about choosing to carry less. It's not a story that makes poverty romantic. Diogenes chose his life, and plenty of people in his world, and ours, don't get to choose. What the Cynics were after wasn't hardship for its own sake. It was freedom. One way to put their point: every thing you own also owns a little of you. It needs storing, protecting, repairing, worrying about. Put it down and your hands are free. That's week five. Rome's hard nights. Cato. Seneca, and life long enough. Seneca. consolatio, Seneca in exile, comforting his mother. imago vitae: Seneca's last hours, and the image of a life. Diogenes. And a cup, thrown away because a child knew better. Hard stories, most of them. And each one asking the same quiet question. When everything else is taken, or given away, what's left? Tomorrow, a new week, and a very different kind of teacher: a wise fool.
screen: `A CHILD DRINKS FROM HIS HANDS.` · `THE TEACHER IS A CHILD.` · `CHOSEN, NOT ROMANTIC.` · `WEEK FIVE: WHAT'S LEFT?` · then, large: `LESS TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then take a slow walk through your home in your mind. The closet. The drawers. The shelf you never look at. Find one thing you don't use and wouldn't miss. Something someone else could use. Picture holding it in your hands, and then picture handing it to them. Notice how your hands feel after. The bell holds the time.
Diogenes, the man who owned almost nothing and still found one more thing to put down, after a child beat him at living simply.
Your line: less to carry. Today, give away the thing you found. That's week five: seven stories of hard nights and open hands. Day thirty-five.

screen: `DAY 35 COUNTS. WEEK FIVE DONE.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING UNDER THE LAMP.`

howItsDone: Many traditions practice voluntary simplicity, from the Cynics and monastic vows of poverty to modern decluttering, giving away what isn't needed so that it can serve someone else.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes. you own a cloak, a stick, a bag and a cup. you watch a child drink water from cupped hands. what do you do?
options: keep the cup. you need something.
fork.reveal: he throws it away, saying a child has beaten him at living simply. later, seeing a boy eat lentils from bread, he throws away his bowl too.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who didn't want a cup.
what it means: even with almost nothing, there's one more thing to put down, and a child can be the teacher.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 6.37 tells both the cup and the bowl; Cynic self-sufficiency was called autarkeia, needing as little as possible.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.37

notes: DL 6.37: cup thrown from his wallet on seeing a child drink from his hands ('A child has beaten me in plainness of living', paraphrased); bowl thrown away on seeing a boy who had broken his dish eat lentils from a hollow loaf. Confirm.
Diogenes's possessions (cloak, staff, wallet/bag, cup) are the traditional Cynic kit (DL 6.22–23); confirm.
Autarkeia (self-sufficiency) as the Cynic ideal; confirm the trapdoor note.
Week-five look-back in the teach and carry; the teach ends by pointing to week six (Nasruddin).

Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Think about...Everyone has one' or 'Now picture'; removed the fountain and the wooden cup (Diogenes Laërtius 6.37 mentions neither) from voice, screen, match and fork; 'every thing you own owns a little of you' is now framed as a way to put the Cynics' point, not as their saying.
